q: The Bobo doll experiment, famously conducted in the 1960s, was done by:
concept: The answer is b: the Bobo doll experiment was conducted by Albert Bandura. Albert Bandura, with Dorothea Ross and Sheila Ross (1961), tested whether children learn aggression simply by watching. Seventy-two nursery-school children, aged about 3 to 6, were taken one at a time to a playroom where an adult model either attacked a large inflatable Bobo doll (punching it, hitting it with a mallet, kicking it and shouting 'Sock him in the nose!') or played quietly with toys; a control group saw no model. Later, after being mildly frustrated, each child was left with toys that included a Bobo doll. Children who had watched the aggressive model copied many of its exact acts and words, and boys showed more physical aggression than girls. No one had rewarded them. A 1963 follow-up showed that filmed and cartoon models worked almost as well as live ones, and a 1965 study showed that seeing the model punished reduced imitation but not learning: once offered a reward, those children reproduced the acts too. These studies founded social learning theory, later social cognitive theory, with its four processes of attention, retention, reproduction and motivation. Example: after watching an older cousin slam a door in anger, little Arjun slams his toy cupboard the same way the next day. Option b is right because Bandura designed and ran the Bobo doll studies at Stanford in the early 1960s. Exam trap: 'James Lange' is not one person but a merged label for the James-Lange theory of emotion (William James, 1884; Carl Lange, 1885), and the other two names are famous psychologists from unrelated fields.

traps.a: James Lange is a garbled merger of William James (1884) and Carl Lange (1885), who independently proposed that emotion is the perception of bodily changes; neither ran any study of imitated aggression.
traps.c: Daniel Kahneman, with Amos Tversky (1974), studied heuristics and biases in judgement and won the 2002 Nobel prize in economics; he did not study the imitation of aggression.
traps.d: Abraham Maslow (1943) proposed the hierarchy of needs and self-actualisation, a humanistic theory of motivation; he ran no observational learning experiments.

q: Adults typically talk to babies in a special way. This has been defined as 'Motherese', 'baby talk register' or 'adult-child speech'. Identify one characteristic of this type of adult-child speech.

options.a: The mean length of utterance is shorter in adult-child speech than it is in adult-adult speech.
options.b: Adults speak much more quickly to babies than they do to other adults.
options.c: Adults pause more frequently when they talk to other adults than they do when they talk to babies.
options.d: Adult-child speech has a lower pitch and a narrower range of pitch.

concept: The correct answer is that the mean length of utterance is shorter in adult-child speech than in adult-adult speech. Motherese, also called infant-directed speech or child-directed speech, is the distinctive register adults spontaneously use when talking to babies. Its well-documented features include a higher overall pitch, an exaggerated and wider pitch range with sing-song intonation, a slower rate of speech, more frequent and longer pauses, clearer enunciation, repetition, and simpler, shorter sentences (a shorter mean length of utterance). The mean length of utterance (MLU), a measure introduced by Roger Brown, is the average number of morphemes per utterance and is a standard index of grammatical complexity; adults naturally shorten it when addressing infants. These modifications are thought to support language acquisition by making speech more salient, easier to segment, and emotionally engaging, capturing and holding the infant's attention. Options B, C, and D each state the reverse of a true feature: speech to babies is slower not quicker, contains more pauses not fewer, and uses higher and more variable pitch not lower and narrower. This item tests whether the student knows the actual acoustic and structural characteristics of infant-directed speech, correctly identifying the shortened utterance length.

traps.b: This is reversed: adults speak more slowly, not more quickly, to babies to aid comprehension.
traps.c: This is reversed: adults pause more frequently and clearly when talking to babies, not to other adults.
traps.d: This is reversed: motherese uses higher pitch and an exaggerated, wider pitch range, not lower pitch with a narrow range.

q: What is the non-parametric alternative to the independent t-test?
concept: The answer is b: the Mann-Whitney U test is the non-parametric alternative to the independent-samples t test. The t test compares the means of two independent groups and assumes interval data, roughly normal distributions and similar variances. When those assumptions fail, for example with ordinal ratings, small samples or badly skewed scores, you switch to a rank test. Henry Mann and Donald Whitney (1947) built the U test: pool the scores of both groups, rank them from lowest to highest, then ask whether one group's ranks run consistently higher than the other's. U counts how often a score in one group beats a score in the other. It is equivalent to the rank-sum test of Frank Wilcoxon (1945). Example: Meera rates the homesickness of 12 hostel students and 10 day scholars on a 1 to 5 scale. The ratings are ordinal and skewed, so she ranks all 22 together and runs Mann-Whitney instead of t. Option b is right because each parametric test has a rank-based partner, and for two independent groups that partner is the Mann-Whitney U test. Exam trap: match the design before the test. Two related samples (paired t) take the Wilcoxon signed-rank test; three or more independent groups (one-way ANOVA) take the Kruskal-Wallis H test (William Kruskal and W. Allen Wallis, 1952); three or more related samples (repeated-measures ANOVA) take the Friedman test (Milton Friedman, 1937). Students who remember only 'Wilcoxon' often pick the signed-rank test for independent groups, which is wrong.

traps.c: MANOVA is a parametric multivariate test comparing groups on two or more dependent variables at once. It adds assumptions (multivariate normality) rather than dropping them.
traps.d: The Wald-Wolfowitz runs test (Abraham Wald and Jacob Wolfowitz, 1940) can compare two independent samples by counting runs in the pooled, ordered scores, but it is a weak, general test of any difference between distributions and is mostly used to check the randomness of a sequence. It is not the standard alternative to the t test.

q: Which of the following does not assess the internal consistency reliability?
concept: The answer is a: test-retest reliability does not assess internal consistency. Reliability is the consistency of scores, and each method catches a different source of error. Test-retest reliability gives the same test to the same people twice, usually a fortnight to a few weeks apart, and correlates the two sets of scores. It yields a coefficient of stability and catches error from changes over time, such as mood, health and testing conditions. Internal consistency methods need only one administration and ask whether the parts of the test agree with each other. Split-half reliability scores two halves (often odd against even items), correlates them, and steps the half-test correlation up to full length with the Spearman-Brown formula, published independently by Charles Spearman and William Brown in 1910. The Kuder-Richardson formulas, KR-20 and KR-21 (G. Frederic Kuder and Marion Richardson, 1937), estimate consistency across all items for items scored right or wrong. Cronbach's alpha (Lee Cronbach, 1951) generalises KR-20 to items with several answer points, such as rating scales, and equals the mean of all possible split-half coefficients. Example: Kabir gives his new exam-anxiety scale once to 200 students and computes alpha to check that the items hang together; a month later he retests them to check stability, which is test-retest reliability. Option a is right because test-retest needs two occasions and measures stability over time, not agreement among items. Exam trap: all four options are reliability methods, so the item turns on which one is about time; parallel (alternate) forms reliability is not internal consistency either, since it measures the equivalence of two forms.

traps.b: Split-half reliability is an internal consistency method: one test, one sitting, two halves correlated and then corrected to full length with the Spearman-Brown formula.
traps.c: The Kuder-Richardson formulas (KR-20 and KR-21, 1937) measure inter-item consistency for dichotomously scored items, so they are internal consistency estimates.
traps.d: Cronbach's alpha (Lee Cronbach, 1951) is the most widely used internal consistency coefficient, the average of all possible split-half coefficients.

q: Which of the following does not fall under the skills of counsellor?
concept: The answer is c: manipulation is not a skill of a counsellor. Counselling skills are learned ways of helping a client explore and resolve a problem. Allen Ivey's microcounselling (late 1960s) teaches them one at a time: attending behaviour (eye contact, posture, tone, following the client's topic), then the basic listening sequence of open and closed questions, encouragers, paraphrasing, reflection of feeling and summarising. Gerard Egan (The Skilled Helper, 1975) adds empathy and challenge. Reflection mirrors back the feeling or meaning behind the client's words ('You sound let down by your friends'). Active listening, described by Carl Rogers and Richard Farson in a 1957 paper of that name, means full attention to words, tone and body language, with responses that show understanding. Accepting the client's feelings is Carl Rogers's unconditional positive regard: valuing the person without judging what he or she feels. Manipulation is steering a person covertly, by pressure, flattery, deceit or guilt, towards ends the counsellor has chosen. It violates the client's autonomy and trust and is an ethical breach, not a skill. Example: when Arjun says he wants to leave engineering for music, his counsellor reflects his excitement and fear and helps him weigh both paths; a manipulative counsellor would quietly play on his guilt about his parents to push him back. Option c is right because it is the only option that serves the counsellor's agenda instead of the client's growth. Exam trap: do not confuse manipulation with legitimate influencing skills such as confrontation (gently pointing out discrepancies), interpretation or giving information, which are open, serve the client and form part of Allen Ivey's hierarchy.

traps.a: Reflection (of feeling or content) is a basic listening microskill in Allen Ivey's sequence and in Carl Rogers's method, so it is a genuine counsellor skill.
traps.b: Active listening (Carl Rogers and Richard Farson, 1957) is the foundation of all counselling skills, not an exception to them.
traps.d: Accepting the client's feelings is unconditional positive regard, one of Carl Rogers's core conditions, and a basic counselling attitude and skill.

q: Delusion is a disorder of:
concept: The answer is b: a delusion is a disorder of thought, specifically of the content of thought. Karl Jaspers (1913), in General Psychopathology, gave the classic marks of a delusion: it is held with extraordinary conviction, it cannot be changed by contrary evidence or argument, and its content is false or impossible. Modern definitions add that it is out of keeping with the person's cultural and educational background, so a belief shared by a whole community, such as faith in a deity, is not a delusion. Psychopathology splits thought disorders into two kinds. Disorders of thought content concern what a person thinks: delusions, overvalued ideas and obsessions. Disorders of thought form concern how thoughts are linked: loosening of associations, flight of ideas, tangentiality, circumstantiality and thought blocking. Common delusional themes are persecutory, grandiose, referential, jealous, nihilistic and somatic. Delusions are a core symptom of schizophrenia and delusional disorder, and they also occur in psychotic depression and mania. For example, Kabir insists that his neighbours are spying on him through cameras hidden in his ceiling fan; when his family opens the fan and shows him it is empty, he says they have been bribed. That fixed false belief is a disorder of thought content. Option b is right because a delusion is a false belief, and beliefs are products of thinking, not of sensing or feeling. Exam trap: hallucinations and delusions are often listed together as psychotic symptoms, but a hallucination (a perception without a stimulus) is a disorder of perception, while a delusion is a disorder of thought.

traps.a: Disorders of perception are hallucinations (perception without a stimulus) and illusions (misperception of a real stimulus); a delusion is a false belief, not a false perception.
traps.c: Disorders of personality are enduring, inflexible patterns of inner experience and behaviour (the personality disorders); a delusion is a symptom of disordered thought, usually in psychosis, not a personality pattern.
traps.d: Disorders of affect concern mood and emotional expression, such as depression, elation, or blunted and incongruent affect; delusions may be coloured by mood but are disorders of thought.

q: Arrange the prominent personalities in clinical psychology in ascending order :

options.a: St. Augustine - Plato - Johann Weyer - William Harvey
options.b: Plato - St. Augustine - William Harvey - Johann Weyer
options.c: Plato - St. Augustine - Johann Weyer - William Harvey
options.d: Plato - Johann Weyer - St. Augustine - William Harvey

concept: The answer is c: in chronological (ascending) order the four are Plato, St. Augustine, Johann Weyer and William Harvey. The question asks you to place figures from the early history of ideas about mental illness on a timeline. Plato (about 427 to 347 BC), the Greek philosopher, saw mental disturbance partly as a loss of harmony in the soul, held that the disturbed should not be judged like others for their acts, and urged in the Laws that families care for them at home. St. Augustine of Hippo (AD 354 to 430) wrote the Confessions (about AD 397 to 400), a searching examination of his own feelings, conflicts and anguish that historians treat as a forerunner of introspection and even of psychoanalytic self-analysis. Johann Weyer (1515 to 1588), a Rhineland physician, argued in De praestigiis daemonum (1563) that many women accused of witchcraft were mentally ill and needed treatment, not burning; Gregory Zilboorg (1941) called him the founder of modern psychiatry. William Harvey (1578 to 1657), the English physician who described the circulation of the blood in De motu cordis (1628), also noted that emotions such as fear and anger disturb the heart, an early psychosomatic idea. A memory hook: Greek philosophy (BC), a Church Father of the late Roman Empire, the Renaissance protest against witch hunts (sixteenth century), then the scientific revolution (seventeenth century). For example, Kabir makes a timeline card: fourth century BC, about AD 400, 1563, 1628. Option c is right because it is the only sequence that follows these dates. Exam trap: Weyer and Harvey were both early modern physicians, so options swap them; but Weyer's book (1563) appeared before Harvey was even born (1578).

traps.a: This puts St. Augustine (AD 354 to 430) before Plato (about 427 to 347 BC), but Plato lived some 750 years earlier, so the first two are reversed.
traps.b: This places William Harvey (De motu cordis, 1628) before Johann Weyer (De praestigiis daemonum, 1563); Weyer's work came first, before Harvey was even born.
traps.d: This puts Johann Weyer, a sixteenth-century Renaissance physician, before St. Augustine, a Church Father of the fourth and fifth centuries AD, breaking the timeline by more than a thousand years.

q: Which of the following is not an attribute of extraversion in the Big Five factor theory of personality?
concept: The answer is c: being self-conscious is not an attribute of extraversion; in the Big Five it is a facet of neuroticism. The Big Five or five-factor model describes personality with five broad traits, remembered as OCEAN: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. They emerged from factor analyses of the trait words in everyday language, first reported by Ernest Tupes and Raymond Christal (1961), and Paul Costa and Robert McCrae (1992) measured them with the NEO-PI-R, which splits each factor into six facets. The extraversion facets are warmth, gregariousness, assertiveness, activity, excitement-seeking and positive emotions. So a high scorer is sociable (gregariousness), talkative (assertiveness and activity) and affectionate (warmth). The neuroticism facets are anxiety, angry hostility, depression, self-consciousness, impulsiveness and vulnerability. Self-consciousness means shyness and embarrassment in front of others, a sensitivity to being judged. Consider Arjun, who chats with everyone at a wedding, hugs his cousins and is first on the dance floor: high extraversion. His cousin Riya worries that people are watching her and blushes when spoken to: that is high self-consciousness, a neuroticism facet. Option c is right because self-consciousness belongs to the neuroticism domain, not to extraversion. Exam trap: self-conscious sounds like the opposite of sociable, so students treat it as low extraversion; but introversion simply means quiet and reserved, while the anxious discomfort of self-consciousness is neuroticism. A calm introvert need not be self-conscious at all.

traps.b: Talkative is a standard marker adjective for extraversion, linked to its assertiveness and activity facets; extraverts talk readily and take the lead.
traps.d: Affectionate matches the warmth facet of extraversion, the friendly closeness extraverts show; it is an extraversion attribute even though it sounds like agreeableness.

q: Which part of the limbic system is involved in an animal's feeling of hunger?
concept: The answer is d: the hypothalamus is the part of the limbic system that controls hunger. The hypothalamus is a small structure below the thalamus that keeps the body's internal balance (homeostasis): hunger, thirst, temperature, sex and the hormones of the pituitary. It is usually counted with the limbic system because it carries out the bodily side of emotion and motivation. Two of its regions were long taught as a dual centre for eating. Albert Hetherington and Stephen Ranson (1940) found that lesions of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) made rats overeat and grow obese, so the VMH was called the satiety centre. Then the Indian physiologist Bal Krishan Anand, working with John Brobeck (1951), showed that lesions of the lateral hypothalamus (LH) made rats stop eating (aphagia) and drinking, to the point of starving unless fed by tube; stimulating the LH made them eat. So the LH became the feeding centre, and Eliot Stellar (1954) built both findings into the dual-centre theory. Modern work adds hormones that act on the hypothalamus, especially its arcuate nucleus: ghrelin from the empty stomach signals hunger, while leptin from fat stores and insulin from the pancreas signal fullness. Option d is right because hunger and satiety signals are integrated in the hypothalamus, chiefly its lateral and ventromedial regions. Exam trap: the classic pairing is easy to reverse. Lateral hypothalamus damage stops eating (it is the feeding or 'start' centre); ventromedial damage causes overeating (it is the satiety or 'stop' centre). Also, the thalamus sounds similar but is a sensory relay, not a drive centre.

traps.a: The thalamus is the sensory relay station (every sense except smell passes through it to the cortex); it does not regulate hunger.
traps.b: The pons is a brainstem structure that relays signals to the cerebellum and helps control breathing and REM sleep; it is not a limbic hunger centre.
traps.c: The hippocampus is the limbic structure for forming new long-term memories and spatial maps, not for hunger.

q: Who is particularly interested in studying patterns of behaviour, beliefs and values which are shared by people?
concept: The answer is a: a social psychologist is the specialist most interested in the patterns of behaviour, beliefs and values that people share. Social psychology is the scientific study of how individuals think, feel and act in relation to other people. Gordon Allport (1954) gave the classic definition: it studies how a person's thoughts, feelings and behaviour are influenced by the actual, imagined or implied presence of others. A social psychologist would study how that shared habit arose and why she adopted it. Subfields such as cultural and cross-cultural psychology push the same question across whole societies. Option a is right because only social psychology takes shared, group-level patterns of thought and action as its central subject. q: The "strange situation" is a test of:
concept: The answer is a: the Strange Situation is a laboratory test of the attachment between an infant and a caregiver. John Bowlby (1969) argued that infants are biologically prepared to form an attachment, a lasting emotional bond, to a caregiver who serves as a secure base. Mary Ainsworth (1969), who had worked with Bowlby, devised the Strange Situation with Barbara Wittig to measure the quality of that bond; the full account came in Patterns of Attachment (1978). A 12 to 18 month old passes through eight short episodes of about three minutes each: exploring a playroom with the caregiver, meeting a stranger, being left with the stranger, a reunion, being left alone, the stranger returning, and a second reunion. Observers score exploration, distress at separation, reaction to the stranger and, above all, behaviour at reunion. Ainsworth found three patterns: secure (type B, about two thirds of her sample: upset when the mother leaves, quickly comforted on her return), insecure-avoidant (type A: little distress, ignores the mother on reunion) and insecure-resistant or ambivalent (type C: very distressed, seeks contact yet angrily resists it). Mary Main and Judith Solomon (1986) added a disorganised pattern (type D). For example, if baby Meera cries when her mother leaves but crawls to her and settles within seconds on reunion, she is classed as securely attached. Option a is right because the procedure was designed specifically to classify the quality of infant attachment. Exam trap: two distractors are Jean Piaget's (1936) terms. Assimilation and accommodation are processes of cognitive adaptation and have nothing to do with the Strange Situation. Also, the Strange Situation is Ainsworth's, not Bowlby's or Harry Harlow's (1958), even though all three studied attachment.

traps.b: Accommodation is Jean Piaget's process of changing an existing scheme to fit new information; it is a cognitive concept, not what the Strange Situation measures.
traps.c: Assimilation is Piaget's process of fitting new information into an existing scheme; it belongs to cognitive development, not attachment.

q: Match the following. a. Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test, b. Kruskal-Wallis Test, c. Eta-squared, d. Friedman Test. 1. Non-parametric equivalent of Repeated Measures ANOVA, 2. Effect size in ANOVA, 3. Non-parametric equivalent of One-way ANOVA, 4. Non-parametric test for two related samples
concept: The answer is a: the correct matches are Wilcoxon signed-rank with two related samples (a-4), Kruskal-Wallis with one-way ANOVA (b-3), eta-squared with effect size in ANOVA (c-2) and Friedman with repeated measures ANOVA (d-1). Non-parametric tests replace raw scores with ranks, so they need no normality assumption and suit ordinal or skewed data. Each has a parametric partner. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Frank Wilcoxon, 1945) is for two related samples, such as the same patients before and after therapy. It ranks the size of each person's difference and reattaches the signs, so it uses both direction and magnitude; it is the rank-based partner of the paired t-test. The Kruskal-Wallis H test (William Kruskal and W. Allen Wallis, 1952) pools and ranks the scores of three or more independent groups and compares their mean ranks, the non-parametric equivalent of one-way ANOVA. The Friedman test, devised by the economist Milton Friedman (1937), ranks each person's scores across three or more conditions and compares the rank totals, the non-parametric equivalent of repeated measures ANOVA. Eta-squared is not a test at all: it is an effect size for ANOVA, the proportion of total variance explained by the factor (sum of squares between groups divided by the total sum of squares). Jacob Cohen (1988) suggested about .01 as small, .06 as medium and .14 as large. Example: Riya rates anxiety in the same 15 patients at weeks 0, 4 and 8 on an ordinal scale, so she uses the Friedman test. Option a is right because it is the only option with all four pairs correct. Exam trap: a-4 appears in both a and d, so decide on b: Kruskal-Wallis is the independent-groups (one-way) equivalent, which rules out d, where it is wrongly matched to repeated measures.

traps.b: This matches Wilcoxon to one-way ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis to effect size and eta-squared to two related samples; only the Friedman pairing (d-1) is right.
traps.c: This swaps the roles: Wilcoxon is not the repeated measures equivalent (that is Friedman), Kruskal-Wallis is not a two related samples test (that is Wilcoxon) and Friedman is not the one-way equivalent (that is Kruskal-Wallis). Only c-2 is right.
traps.d: Wilcoxon (a-4) is right, but Kruskal-Wallis is for independent groups, not repeated measures; eta-squared is an effect size, not a test; and Friedman is not an effect size.

q: When the reliability coefficient of a test is 1.00, the standard error of measurement will be:
concept: The answer is b: when the reliability coefficient is 1.00, the standard error of measurement (SEM) is 0. A reliability coefficient describes how consistent a group's scores are; the SEM turns that into the likely error in one person's score. It is the standard deviation of the scores a person would obtain over many imaginary retestings, spread around their true score. The formula is SEM = SD x square root of (1 minus r), where SD is the standard deviation of the test scores and r is the reliability coefficient. With r = 1, 1 minus r is 0, its square root is 0, and the SEM is 0: every observed score equals the true score, with no measurement error at all. At the other extreme, with r = 0, the SEM equals the SD, because the score is pure error. In between, the SEM shrinks as reliability rises. Example: on an IQ test with SD 15 and reliability 0.91, SEM = 15 x 0.30 = 4.5, so if Meera scores 110, her true score lies between 105.5 and 114.5 about 68 percent of the time. Option b is right because perfect reliability leaves no error to estimate. Exam trap: students see 1.00 in the stem and pick 1.00, or assume SEM and reliability move together; they move in opposite directions.

traps.c: 0.50 does not follow from perfect reliability; it would need a reliability below 1 (for example r = 0.75 with an SD of 1).
traps.d: "None of these" fails because 0 is listed and is the exact answer.

q: The following is NOT a principle in the Counselling process:

options.a: Include client's family members if needed
options.b: Respecting the bizarre feelings of the client
options.c: Helping client develop a positive attitude

concept: The answer is d: making decisions for the client breaks a basic principle of counselling. Counselling is a helping relationship in which a trained person helps a client understand a problem and find his or her own way through it. Carl Rogers (1951), in Client-Centered Therapy, argued that the client, not the counsellor, is the expert on his own life and has an inborn drive towards growth; the counsellor's job is to provide empathy, unconditional positive regard and genuineness. Felix Biestek (1957) set out seven principles of the casework relationship that counselling shares: individualisation, purposeful expression of feelings, controlled emotional involvement, acceptance, a non-judgemental attitude, client self-determination and confidentiality. Client self-determination means the client makes the final choices. Deciding for him breeds dependence, removes his ownership of the outcome and lets the counsellor's values take over. The other options fit accepted practice: accept and respect all of the client's feelings, even odd or 'bizarre' ones; involve the family when the problem or its solution lies partly in the family; and help the client build a hopeful, positive attitude. Example: Arjun, 22, cannot decide whether to take a job in Bengaluru or stay home to care for his ageing parents. A good counsellor helps him weigh the pros and cons, explore his values and feelings, and perhaps meets the parents too. She does not tell him 'take the job'. Option d is right because counselling respects client self-determination; decisions belong to the client. Exam trap: advice-giving and directive guidance are older styles, so 'deciding for the client' can sound helpful. In counselling it is a violation, not a technique.

traps.b: Respecting the client's feelings, however odd or 'bizarre', reflects acceptance and a non-judgemental attitude (Felix Biestek, 1957) and Carl Rogers's unconditional positive regard. It is a core principle, not a violation.
traps.c: Helping the client develop a positive, hopeful attitude is a recognised aim; Jerome Frank (1961) named the arousal of hope as a common factor in all effective therapies. It fits counselling, so it is not the answer.

q: A disorder of neural development characterised by impaired social interaction and communication, and by restricted and repetitive behaviour, is:
concept: The answer is d: a disorder of neural development marked by impaired social interaction, impaired communication and restricted, repetitive behaviour is a pervasive developmental disorder (PDD), the older name for what is now autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Lorna Wing and Judith Gould (1979) called these three features the triad of impairments. Leo Kanner (1943) first described infantile autism in eleven children with extreme aloneness and an anxious insistence on sameness, and Hans Asperger (1944) described more verbally able children. DSM-IV (1994) and ICD-10 (1992) grouped these conditions as pervasive developmental disorders: autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, Rett's disorder, childhood disintegrative disorder and PDD not otherwise specified. 'Pervasive' meant the problems touch almost every area of the child's life. DSM-5 (2013) merged most of them into a single autism spectrum disorder with two symptom domains: persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, and restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities, present from early childhood. Example: four-year-old Kabir avoids eye contact, does not point to share interest, lines up his toy cars in the same order every day and screams if the order is changed. This is autism, a pervasive developmental disorder. Option d is right because the stem lists exactly the defining triad of autism, and PDD is the diagnostic family autism belonged to. Exam trap: intellectual disability (a) and the genetic syndromes (b and c) often occur alongside autism and so tempt, but they are defined by low intelligence and physical features, not by the social, communication and repetitive-behaviour triad. Older papers still say PDD where DSM-5 says autism spectrum disorder.

traps.a: Mental retardation (now intellectual disability) is defined by deficits in intellectual and adaptive functioning beginning in the developmental period, not by the social and repetitive-behaviour triad, though many autistic children also have it.
traps.b: Down syndrome is a chromosomal condition (trisomy 21, described by John Langdon Down in 1866) with typical facial features and intellectual disability; social interest is often relatively good, so it does not match the stem.
traps.c: Cat's cry (cri du chat) syndrome is a deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5 (Jerome Lejeune, 1963) causing a high cat-like cry, a small head and severe intellectual disability; it is a genetic syndrome, not the autism triad.

q: What is the primary focus of Indian psychology?

options.a: The application of Western psychological theories exclusively.
options.b: The promotion of meditation without psychological context.
options.c: The study of Indian folklore and mythology.
options.d: The integration of Indian philosophical traditions with psychological concepts.

concept: Indian psychology is an approach to psychology that draws on the classical Indian philosophical and contemplative traditions, such as the Vedas, Upanishads, the Yoga system of Patanjali, Samkhya, Buddhism, and the Bhagavad Gita, and integrates their concepts and methods with modern psychological inquiry. Its primary focus is the systematic study of mind, consciousness, self (atman), and human potential as understood within these indigenous traditions, and the application of that understanding to psychological questions. It emphasizes consciousness, self-realization, and holistic, spiritually informed models of well-being, and it treats practices such as meditation and yoga not as isolated techniques but as embedded within a coherent theory of mind and liberation. Scholars such as Girishwar Misra, K. Ramakrishna Rao, and R. M. Matthijs Cornelissen have helped articulate it as a distinct field. The distractors mischaracterize it: it does not apply only Western theories, it does not promote meditation without context, and it is not merely the study of folklore. Because Indian psychology is defined by integrating Indian philosophical traditions with psychological concepts, option d is correct.

traps.a: Indian psychology is defined precisely by drawing on indigenous traditions, not by applying Western theories exclusively.
traps.b: It situates practices such as meditation within a rich psychological and philosophical framework, not without context.
traps.c: It is grounded in philosophical and contemplative traditions, not merely folklore and mythology.

q: Personality psychologists such as Cattell, Spearman, Eysenck all used factor analysis in their work, as they felt this was more objective method of developing trait taxonomies. However this method is criticised for which of the following reasons?

options.c: Choosing terms to enter into the analysis

concept: The answer is d: factor analysis is criticised on all three counts: the researcher chooses what goes in, decides how many factors to keep, and names them. Factor analysis is a statistical method that takes the correlations among many measures and finds a few underlying factors that explain them. Charles Spearman (1904) invented it to show a general intelligence factor, g. Raymond Cattell (1905 to 1998) applied it to trait words and ratings and arrived at 16 source traits (the 16PF, 1949); Hans Eysenck (1916 to 1997) arrived at three superfactors (extraversion, neuroticism, psychoticism); later researchers found five. The disagreement comes from three points of judgement. (1) Input: the result depends on which variables or trait terms enter the analysis; leave out a domain and no factor for it can appear (garbage in, garbage out). (2) Number of factors: how many to keep is a decision, guided by rules such as Henry Kaiser's eigenvalue-greater-than-one rule or Cattell's scree test (1966), and different rules give different answers. (3) Naming: a factor is only a cluster of loadings; calling it 'anxiety' or 'neuroticism' is the researcher's interpretation. Example: Kabir factor-analyses 40 adjectives; if he leaves out every word about honesty, no honesty factor can emerge, however important honesty is in real life. Option d is right because a, b and c are all standard criticisms of the method. Exam trap: each single option is true, so a student who spots one valid criticism may stop there; with three true statements, 'All of the above' is the answer.

traps.a: Choosing factor names is a real criticism (a factor is only a pattern of loadings and the label is the researcher's interpretation), but picking it alone misses the equally standard problems of deciding how many factors exist and choosing what to enter.
traps.b: Deciding how many factors exist is a real criticism (Kaiser's rule, Cattell's scree test and other rules can give different numbers, hence 16 versus 3 versus 5), but on its own it leaves out naming and the choice of input.
traps.c: Choosing the terms to enter is a real criticism (the factors can only reflect the variables put in), but on its own it leaves out the naming and number-of-factors problems, which are just as standard.

q: Which of the following is an invasive method used in physiological psychology?
concept: The answer is c: lesion techniques are an invasive method in physiological psychology. A method is invasive when it enters the body or skull or damages tissue. A lesion study destroys or removes a small part of the brain and infers that part's job from what the animal, or patient, can no longer do. In animals a stereotaxic instrument holds the head and guides an electrode to precise coordinates; tissue is then destroyed by suction (aspiration), radio-frequency current, a knife cut or a neurotoxin such as 6-hydroxydopamine, which kills dopamine and noradrenaline neurons. Albert Hetherington and Stephen Ranson (1940) lesioned the ventromedial hypothalamus of rats, which then overate and became obese, and Karl Lashley (1929) removed different amounts of rat cortex in his search for the memory trace. In humans the lesion method studies damage caused by stroke, injury or surgery: Paul Broca (1861) linked the lost speech of his patient 'Tan' to damage in the left frontal lobe. EEG, by contrast, records the brain's electrical activity from electrodes on the scalp (Hans Berger, 1929). MRI uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to image brain structure, and fMRI tracks changes in blood oxygen to show which areas are active; both work from outside the head. Example: Kavya, a research student, makes a small lesion in a rat's amygdala and finds that the rat no longer freezes to a tone that used to signal shock. Option c is right because lesioning physically damages brain tissue, the defining feature of an invasive method. Exam trap: transcranial magnetic stimulation is called a 'virtual lesion' but is non-invasive, and PET is the imaging method that needs an injected radioactive tracer; do not label MRI or fMRI invasive just because the machines are powerful.

traps.a: EEG (Hans Berger, 1929) picks up summed electrical activity through electrodes on the scalp; nothing enters the skull, so it is non-invasive.
traps.b: MRI images brain structure with a magnetic field and radio waves from outside the head; it involves no surgery or radiation and is non-invasive.
traps.d: fMRI measures the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal as an index of neural activity; like structural MRI it is non-invasive.

q: Which function of communication is illustrated when a person rolls his or her eyes while making a negative comment about another?
concept: The answer is b: rolling the eyes while making a negative comment illustrates accenting, a nonverbal cue that emphasises part of a verbal message. Nonverbal behaviour (face, eyes, gesture, posture, voice) works alongside words. Mark Knapp (1972), building on Paul Ekman's work in the 1960s, listed six functions it can serve in relation to speech. Repeating restates the words (saying 'go straight' and pointing ahead). Complementing adds to or fits the words (a sad face while apologising). Substituting replaces words (a nod for yes, a shrug with no speech). Accenting stresses or underlines the words (banging the table on 'never', a raised tone on a key word). Regulating manages the flow of conversation (nodding to keep someone talking, raising a hand to take a turn, looking away to signal the end). Contradicting sends a message opposite to the words ('I'm fine' said through tears). Eye-rolling during a negative remark points the same way as the words and intensifies their scorn, so it accents them. Example: Kabir says 'Rohan's presentation was a disaster' and rolls his eyes on 'disaster'; the roll does not replace, regulate or contradict his words, it underlines his contempt. Option b is right because the eye-roll emphasises the negative message the person is already giving. Exam trap: contradicting (d) is chosen because eye-rolling is famous as a sign of sarcasm; it would contradict only if the words were positive, such as 'great idea' with an eye-roll, but with a negative comment the two channels agree.

q: Psychologists and psychiatrists have often viewed adolescence as a time when the healthy trajectory of development involves detachment from the parents. Today, however, there is a greater awareness that:

options.a: it can be healthy for interdependence to continue
options.b: detachment typically occurs earlier, in middle childhood
options.c: the peer group is more important than parents
options.d: all parents have the same goal for their adolescent child

concept: The correct answer is that it can be healthy for interdependence to continue. Older psychoanalytic views, notably those of Anna Freud and Peter Blos, portrayed adolescence as requiring detachment or emotional separation from parents, treating strong parental ties in the teen years as a sign of immaturity. Contemporary developmental research, associated with figures such as Laurence Steinberg and attachment-informed scholars, has revised this picture. It shows that healthy adolescent development involves individuation and growing autonomy while maintaining warm, connected relationships with parents, that is, a shift toward interdependence rather than a clean break. Secure attachment to parents, in the tradition of John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth, continues to serve as a base from which adolescents explore, and connectedness predicts better adjustment, self-esteem, and identity formation. Autonomy and relatedness are thus complementary, not opposed. This also reflects cultural awareness: many collectivist cultures never framed adolescence as detachment at all. So the modern understanding is that ongoing interdependence, adolescents becoming more autonomous while staying emotionally close to their families, is healthy, which is why option a is correct and the detachment-centered alternatives are outdated.

traps.b: The trend is not that detachment happens earlier; the shift is away from viewing detachment as necessary at all.
traps.c: Modern research does not conclude that peers simply outweigh parents; both remain influential in different domains.
traps.d: Parents plainly differ in goals across families and cultures, so this generalization is false.

q: Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer from the code given below. List-I (Interviews): A. Structured interviews, B. Unstructured interviews, C. Focused interviews, D. Clinical interviews. List-II (Meaning): 1. Greater flexibility approach, 2. Attention on the questions to be answered, 3. Individual life experience, 4. Pre-determined question, 5. Non-directive
concept: The answer is a: A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3. This matching follows C. R. Kothari (2004), Research Methodology: Methods and Techniques, a standard Indian research methods text. Interviews differ in how much is fixed in advance. A structured interview uses a set of predetermined questions with fixed wording and order, often read from a schedule; answers are easy to compare and score, but the method is rigid (A-4). An unstructured interview fixes only the aim and lets the interviewer change the order, wording and follow-up of questions, so its mark is greater flexibility, gaining depth at the cost of comparability (B-1). The focused interview, described by Robert Merton and Patricia Kendall (1946), focuses attention on a given experience of the respondent, such as watching a film or living through a disaster, and on its effects; the interviewer decides the manner and sequence of questions while keeping attention on the issues to be answered (C-2). The clinical interview is concerned with broad underlying feelings or motives, or with the course of the individual's life experience, as when a psychologist takes a developmental history (D-3). Kothari also lists the non-directive interview, in which the interviewer simply encourages the respondent to talk with a bare minimum of direct questioning, a style drawn from the counselling of Carl Rogers (1942); it is the extra item 5 that matches nothing. Example: Sneha studies a cyclone's impact on fishermen. She asks all 200 the same 20 questions (structured), chats freely with village elders (unstructured), asks survivors specifically about the night of the storm and how it changed them (focused), and traces one man's whole life story (clinical). Option a is right because it pairs each interview type with its defining feature. Exam trap: 'non-directive' sounds like unstructured, but here it is the spare distractor; flexibility is what defines the unstructured interview.

traps.b: This gives structured interviews the focused interview's feature and unstructured interviews predetermined questions, reversing the basic fixed versus flexible contrast.
traps.c: This pairs structured interviews with non-directive, the opposite of a fixed schedule, and gives focused interviews predetermined questions; item 5 matches none of the four types.
traps.d: This gives structured interviews flexibility and clinical interviews predetermined questions, again reversing the fixed versus flexible contrast, and uses the non-directive distractor for focused interviews.

q: All of the following statements (except for one) can characterize a professional helping relationship. Which ONE statement does NOT represent a professional helping relationship?

options.a: A helping relationship is initially structured by the counselor or therapist but is open to cooperative restructuring based upon the needs of the client
options.b: A helping relationship is simply one in which one person does something for the other
options.c: A helping relationship is one in which all persons involved perceive the existence of trust, caring, concern, and commitment and act accordingly
options.d: A helping relationship is one that provides for the personal growth of all persons involved

concept: The answer is b: a professional helping relationship is not simply one in which one person does something for the other. Carl Rogers (1958) defined a helping relationship as one in which at least one party intends to promote the growth, development, maturity, improved functioning and improved coping of the other. Counselling texts list its marks. It is structured at first by the counsellor or therapist (time, place, roles, confidentiality, goals), but the structure is open to cooperative revision as the client's needs become clear. All the people involved perceive trust, caring, concern and commitment, and act on them. And it allows personal growth for everyone in it, the helper included, who learns and develops through the work. What it is not is a one-way service in which the helper takes over and fixes things. Doing things for clients breeds dependence and tells them they cannot cope, which defeats the aim of helping. Gerard Egan, in The Skilled Helper (1975), framed the goal as helping clients manage their own problems and develop unused resources. Example: Meera, a counsellor, could phone her client Ananya's college to sort out an attendance problem; instead she helps Ananya plan and rehearse the conversation, and Ananya makes the call herself, gaining confidence for next time. Option b is right because a helping relationship is collaborative and growth-focused, not one person doing something for another. Exam trap: b matches the everyday meaning of helping, which is why it slips past candidates in a NOT item; in counselling, helping means enabling the client, not acting on the client's behalf.

traps.a: This is true of a helping relationship: the counsellor sets the initial structure (roles, time, confidentiality) but reshapes it cooperatively as the client's needs emerge.
traps.c: This is true: mutual trust, caring, concern and commitment, felt and acted on by everyone involved, are defining qualities of the relationship.
traps.d: This is true: a helping relationship fosters growth for all involved, including the helper, in line with Carl Rogers's growth-centred view.

q: Match List I (Disorder) with List II (Symptoms): a. Generalized Anxiety disorder, b. Dementia, c. Schizophrenia, d. Complex partial. 1. Insidious or sudden onset, 2. Deja vu, 3. Elevated blink rate, 4. Persistent worry
concept: The answer is b: a-4, b-1, c-3, d-2, pairing generalised anxiety disorder with persistent worry, dementia with insidious or sudden onset, schizophrenia with an elevated blink rate, and complex partial seizures with deja vu. Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is defined by persistent, excessive worry about many everyday matters that is hard to control, on more days than not for at least 6 months in DSM-5, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension or poor sleep. Dementia is an acquired decline in memory and other cognitive abilities that disrupts daily life, and its onset depends on the cause. Alzheimer's disease begins insidiously and progresses gradually, whereas vascular dementia often starts suddenly after a stroke and worsens stepwise, so 'insidious or sudden onset' covers the dementias as a group. In schizophrenia, the spontaneous eye blink rate is raised in many unmedicated patients; because blinking rises with central dopamine activity, studies from the late 1970s onward read it as a sign of dopamine overactivity, and it tends to fall with antipsychotic treatment. Complex partial seizures (now called focal impaired awareness seizures) usually arise in the temporal lobe. They often begin with an aura such as deja vu, the feeling that a new moment has been lived before, or a rising feeling in the stomach; then the person stares, loses awareness and shows automatisms such as lip smacking. Kabir, 30, suddenly feels he has lived this exact moment before, then stares blankly and fumbles with his shirt for a minute, remembering nothing afterwards. Option b is right because it is the only option that gets all four pairs. Exam trap: deja vu tempts as an odd experience for schizophrenia, but as a brief, stereotyped aura it points to temporal lobe epilepsy.

traps.a: This keeps b-1 and d-2 but swaps the other two: an elevated blink rate is not a GAD sign (a-3), and persistent worry is the core of GAD, not of schizophrenia (c-4).
traps.c: Only b-1 is right here: the blink rate belongs to schizophrenia, not GAD (a-3); deja vu is the temporal lobe seizure aura, not a schizophrenia sign (c-2); and persistent worry is GAD, not complex partial seizures (d-4).
traps.d: This gets a-4 and b-1 but swaps the last two: deja vu belongs to complex partial seizures, not schizophrenia (c-2), and the elevated blink rate belongs to schizophrenia, not epilepsy (d-3).

q: In classical conditioning, a neutral stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus when:

options.a: It is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus
options.b: It is reinforced with a reward
options.c: It is associated with a punishment

concept: Classical conditioning, discovered by the Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov, is a form of associative learning in which a previously neutral stimulus comes to elicit a response after being paired with a stimulus that naturally produces that response. The key terms are: the unconditioned stimulus (UCS), which automatically triggers an unlearned unconditioned response (UCR), such as food (UCS) producing salivation (UCR); and the neutral stimulus, such as a bell, which initially elicits no relevant response. When the neutral stimulus is repeatedly paired with the unconditioned stimulus, it gradually becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS) that, on its own, elicits a learned conditioned response (CR), the bell alone eventually producing salivation. The pairing of the neutral stimulus with the UCS is therefore the essential mechanism, and factors such as contingency and timing (contiguity) matter. The distractors describe operant conditioning of B. F. Skinner (reinforcement with reward, association with punishment) or a condition that prevents learning (random occurrence). Because a neutral stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus through repeated pairing with an unconditioned stimulus, option a is correct.

traps.b: Reinforcement with a reward is the mechanism of operant conditioning, not classical conditioning.
traps.c: Association with punishment likewise concerns operant conditioning, not the pairing that defines classical conditioning.
traps.d: Random occurrence prevents the systematic pairing needed to form a conditioned association.

q: Biologically based characteristic way of reacting is known as
concept: Temperament is the biologically based, early-appearing style of emotional and behavioural reactivity: how intensely, how quickly and in what mood a person tends to respond. The NCERT Class XII Psychology glossary, the likely source of this item, defines temperament exactly as a 'biologically based characteristic way of reacting'. In the same list, trait is a stable, persistent and specific way of behaving, disposition is a tendency to react to a given situation in a characteristic way, and character is the overall pattern of regularly occurring behaviour. The idea is ancient: Hippocrates and Galen linked four temperaments (sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic) to bodily humours. Modern work began with Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess (1977), whose New York Longitudinal Study rated infants on nine dimensions, such as activity level, rhythmicity, approach-withdrawal, adaptability, intensity and mood, and grouped them as easy, difficult or slow-to-warm-up. They stressed goodness of fit between a child's temperament and the demands of the parents. Jerome Kagan later described behavioural inhibition, a shy, wary response to novelty visible in infancy. Twin studies show temperament is moderately heritable, and it is the base on which adult personality is built. Robert Cloninger (1993) made the contrast explicit: temperament is heritable, automatic emotional responding, whereas character develops through learning and self-concept. Example: baby Ishaan cries loudly at every new face and takes weeks to settle into a new routine, an early, inborn reaction style. Option d is right because temperament is the only term defined by its biological basis; the others describe behaviour patterns without that claim.

traps.a: In the NCERT glossary, disposition is a tendency of a person to react to a given situation in a characteristic way. The phrase 'characteristic way of reacting' overlaps almost word for word with the stem, which is exactly why it tempts. The deciding words are 'biologically based': disposition says nothing about where the tendency comes from, and it is used loosely for learned as well as inborn tendencies. Only temperament carries the biological claim.
traps.b: Character is defined in NCERT as the overall pattern of regularly occurring behaviour, and in everyday usage it carries moral evaluation: honesty, self-control, integrity. It is shaped by upbringing, culture and values, so it is learned rather than inborn. Robert Cloninger (1993) set character (self-directedness, cooperativeness, self-transcendence) against temperament on exactly this basis. It tempts because people speak of someone's character as their fundamental nature.
traps.c: A trait is a stable, persistent and specific way of behaving, the basic unit for Gordon Allport (1937), Raymond Cattell (16PF, 1949) and the Big Five. Traits do have a heritable part, so the option is tempting. But a trait is defined descriptively, by consistency across time and situations, not by its biological origin. Temperament is narrower and earlier: it appears in infancy and is the biological core from which adult traits partly develop.
